recall_prompt: Say how you would find n when n plus 1 P 5 to n P 5 is 3 to 2.
insider_note: Four of the five factors are common, so the ratio collapses to (n + 1)/(n − 4) = 3/2. Keep the sides in order when cross-multiplying: the swapped version 3(n + 1) = 2(n − 4) gives n = −11.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write the ratio and cancel
steps.margin_note: First mark. ⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾P₅ = (n + 1)n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3) and ⁿP₅ = n(n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3)(n − 4). Four factors cancel.
steps.memory_tip: Both have five factors and four are shared. Only (n + 1) on top and (n − 4) below survive.

recall.must_convey: That writing both permutations as products and cancelling the four common factors leaves n plus 1 over n minus 4 equal to 3 over 2.
accept: write both as products, four factors cancel, leaving n plus one over n minus four equals three by two
cancel n into n minus one into n minus two into n minus three from both to get n plus one by n minus four
the ratio reduces to n plus one over n minus four
common factors cancel chesthe n plus one by n minus four equal three by two

steps.why: The two permutations share four consecutive factors; only the first factor of the top (n + 1) and the last factor of the bottom (n − 4) survive. The ratio then contains n once on each side.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the 5 in P₅ as a factor — ⁿP₅ has no factor 5.
Writing ⁿP₅ with four factors and losing (n − 4).

steps.label: Cross-multiply and solve
steps.memory_tip: Cross-multiply in order: 2(n + 1) = 3(n − 4), so n = 14. Swapping the sides gives −11.

recall.must_convey: That cross-multiplying gives 2n plus 2 equals 3n minus 12, so n = 14.
accept: two n plus two equals three n minus twelve so n is fourteen
cross multiply to get n equals fourteen

steps.why: Once the ratio is a single fraction in n, cross-multiplying gives a linear equation, so there is exactly one n and no root to reject.
common_mistakes: Writing 3(n + 1) = 2(n − 4) with the sides swapped, giving n = −11.
